screens.heading: Who represents you
screens.body: The officer will ask about the people you will help elect — questions like:
screens.afterQuote: This lesson will help you answer those questions.
screens.coverageLine: It covers 23 of the 128 — the biggest single lesson.
screens.afterTest: After you naturalize, you vote for every one of these jobs.

screens.question: California has about 39 million people. Wyoming has about half a million. In Congress, should California's voice be 78 times louder?
screens.feedback: In 1787 the states nearly walked away from each other over exactly this question. Their compromise built Congress — and it is worth understanding, because it explains six test answers at once.

bodyList: Imagine five towns that share one road, one water supply, and one school.
One town is large; four are small. When they meet to decide things together, how should the voting work?
If every decision follows population, the four small towns are ignored forever — outvoted before they speak.
If every town gets one equal vote, the large town is outvoted by neighbours a fraction of its size.
bodyList2: So groups like this often use both: some decisions counted one way, some the other.
screens.closing: America's Congress is that compromise, made permanent.

cards.example: A representative represents the people of one district.
Everyone on your street is in your district.

cards.def: how long a leader serves before the next election.
cards.example: A senator's term is six years.

paragraphs: Inside the Capitol are two rooms, built on two opposite principles — on purpose.

The Senate: every state equal. Two senators per state, big or small. 50 states × 2 = 100 senators. A senator represents the people of their whole state and serves six years — a longer term than representatives get. Why two per state? Equal representation for small states — the deal that saved the union in 1787, called the Great Compromise.

The House of Representatives: every person equal. Seats follow population — more people, more representatives. 435 voting members. A representative serves the people of one district and serves only two years. Why so short? So they must face the voters constantly — to more closely follow public opinion.
screens.handle: One state, two kinds of voice.
screens.alt: The United States Capitol building, with its two wings marked as the Senate chamber and the House chamber.

paragraphs: The President is elected for four years — and may serve only two terms.
Why the limit? The 22nd Amendment — and you already know the deeper reason: to keep the president from becoming too powerful. The fear of kings, again.
Who actually decides the winner? The Electoral College — a compromise between electing the president by popular vote and letting Congress choose.
screens.resolution: And if the President can no longer serve, the Vice President becomes President.

screens.heading: Two rooms, two kinds of fairness — both true at once.
screens.example: Wyoming's two senators can stand equal to California's two — while in the House, California sends dozens of representatives, because it has far more people. Both truths, both rooms.
screens.nonExample: Imagine only one room, seats by population alone. The five biggest states could outvote the other forty-five on everything, forever. The small states saw that future in 1787 and refused it.
screens.takeaway: That refusal is why the Senate exists.

screens.heading: Two jobs on the test sound alike. Do not mix them up.

termA.name: Senator
termA.def: represents an entire state. Two per state, six-year term.

termB.name: Representative
termB.def: represents one district within a state. 435 in all, two-year term.

screens.resolution: That is the difference the test cares about — everything else follows from it.
